# DeadReckon - Release Trust Rider (signed artifacts, provenance, fail-closed publishing)

This rider holds the prescriptive constraints for the goal at `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/docs/goals/2026-06-01-1523-deadreckon-release-trust-goal.md`. It supersedes nothing in the 2026-05-11 distribution rider; that rider made DeadReckon installable and self-updatable. This rider hardens the official release path so published artifacts are complete, signed where the platform supports it, provenance-backed, and refused when trust material is missing.

**All paths absolute.** Source root is `/Users/gdc/deadreckon`. Runtime state under `/Users/gdc/.deadreckon` is not part of this goal. Release artifacts are created by CI under `target/distrib` and by local tests under tempdirs only.

## Posture (decided - do not redesign)

- **Maturity stays production-release track.** This is release trust hardening, not a new install channel or CLI UX redesign.
- **No DeadReckon durable runtime schema changes.** Do not change `PipelineState`, plans, campaigns, chains, library artifacts, run markers, or install receipts unless an existing release script already owns that file.
- **Official releases fail closed.** On the canonical repository, RC and stable tags must not publish if required signing/provenance/checksum steps fail or required secrets are absent.
- **Forks and PRs remain usable.** Pull requests, branches, and forked repos can run `dist plan` and non-publishing checks without Apple/npm/Homebrew/Windows secrets.
- **No agent-driven publishing.** The agent must not run `git tag`, `git push`, `gh release upload`, `npm publish`, or Homebrew tap pushes outside tests/dry-runs.
- **No new package manager channel.** Stay with cargo-dist installers, GitHub Releases, Homebrew, npm wrapper/platform packages, and the existing update channel model.
- **No secret material in git.** Docs may name secret keys and commands, but not actual values, certificates, passwords, or team identifiers.
- **Edits stay inside `/Users/gdc/deadreckon`.**

- `/Users/gdc/deadreckon/.github/workflows/release.yml`

Important gap: signing before `dist build` is suspicious. If `dist build` rebuilds the binary after the manual signing step, the uploaded artifact may not be the signed binary. The implementation must prove the artifact inside each macOS archive is signed after packaging, or move signing to a position that signs the exact artifact contents.

The hard truth about Apple signing: **almost every step requires a human at a GUI or logged into Apple's portal.** I have no access to your Apple account, your Keychain, or your browser. Here's the honest breakdown.

## Step-by-step

### Step 1 — Create the certificate 👤
Go to **developer.apple.com/account → Certificates → +**. Pick **Developer ID Application** (not "Apple Development", not "Mac App Distribution" — those won't notarize for outside-the-App-Store distribution). You'll be asked for a CSR (Certificate Signing Request).

To make the CSR: **Keychain Access → menu → Certificate Assistant → Request a Certificate From a Certificate Authority** → "Saved to disk". Upload that `.certSigningRequest` to Apple, download the resulting `.cer`, and double-click it to install into your **login** keychain.

> Tip: I *cannot* do the CSR for you — it's a GUI flow that generates a private key inside your keychain.

### Step 2 — Export as `.p12` 👤
In **Keychain Access**, find your "Developer ID Application: …" cert. Expand the disclosure triangle so the **private key** shows underneath it. Select **both** the cert and the key → right-click → **Export 2 items** → format **Personal Information Exchange (.p12)**. It'll ask for a password — **remember it, that's your `APPLE_CERT_PWD`.** Save as e.g. `~/developer-id.p12`.

> If you can't expand to see a private key, the export is useless — CI needs the key to sign. That means the cert was created on a different machine than where the key lives.

### Step 3 — Base64 it 🤖
Once the `.p12` exists, tell me the path and I'll run this for you (it copies the value to your clipboard so it never passes through chat):

```bash
base64 -i ~/developer-id.p12 | tr -d '\n' | pbcopy
```

That clipboard value = `APPLE_CERT_P12`. **Don't paste it to me** — paste it straight into GitHub.

### Step 4 — App-specific password 👤
At **appleid.apple.com → Sign-In and Security → App-Specific Passwords → +**. Label it "deadreckon notarytool". The generated `abcd-efgh-ijkl-mnop` string = `APPLE_APP_PWD`. (This is *not* your Apple account password — notarytool rejects the real one.)

### Step 5 — Team ID 👤
**developer.apple.com/account → Membership details** → the 10-character "Team ID" = `APPLE_TEAM_ID`. `APPLE_ID` is just your Apple login email.

### Step 6 — Add the five GitHub secrets 👤
Web UI: repo → **Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions → New repository secret**, five times. Or via CLI (you run these — they prompt for the value without echoing, and never touch this chat):

```bash
gh secret set APPLE_CERT_P12      # paste the base64 blob
gh secret set APPLE_CERT_PWD      # the .p12 export password
gh secret set APPLE_ID            # your Apple ID email
gh secret set APPLE_TEAM_ID       # 10-char team id
gh secret set APPLE_APP_PWD       # the app-specific password
```

> Your `release.yml:109-121` is fail-soft on these: if `APPLE_CERT_P12` is missing it logs `::warning::` and **skips** signing. Note the release-trust rider says official RC/stable tags should **fail closed** when secrets are absent on the canonical repo — that's a separate gap the rider is tracking, not something the secrets themselves fix.

You're in the right place — but **don't click "Create a certificate" yet.** Apple will immediately ask you to upload a **CSR** (Certificate Signing Request), and you need to make that first. The CSR is what generates your private key locally — and that private key is the thing CI ultimately needs.

## First: make the CSR (Keychain Access)

1. Open **Keychain Access** (⌘-Space → "Keychain Access").
2. Menu bar → **Keychain Access → Certificate Assistant → Request a Certificate From a Certificate Authority…**
3. Fill in:
   - **User Email Address:** your Apple ID email (`greg@specstory.com`)
   - **Common Name:** anything, e.g. "DeadReckon Developer ID"
   - **CA Email Address:** leave blank
   - Select **"Saved to disk"** (not "Emailed to the CA")
4. Click **Continue** → save `CertificateSigningRequest.certSigningRequest` to your Desktop.

> This silently creates a matching **private key** in your login keychain. That pairing is the whole point — without it the cert from Apple is useless for signing.

## Then: back on this screen

5. Click **Create a certificate** (the blue button you see).
6. Under **Software**, pick **Developer ID Application**.
   - ⚠️ Not "Apple Development", not "Developer ID Installer", not "Mac App Distribution". Only **Developer ID Application** notarizes for distribution outside the App Store.
   - If Apple asks for a **profile type / G2 sub-CA**, accept the default ("Developer ID Application Managed" or the standard one is fine).
7. **Upload** the `.certSigningRequest` file from step 4.
8. Click **Continue → Download**. You get a `developer_id_application.cer`.
9. **Double-click the `.cer`** to install it into your login keychain.

## Verify it landed (🤖 I'll run this)

Once you've double-clicked the `.cer`, tell me and I'll confirm the identity is valid locally:

```bash
security find-identity -v -p codesigning | grep "Developer ID Application"
```

When that prints a line with a 40-char hash and "Developer ID Application: …", you're ready for the `.p12` export (the Keychain "export 2 items" step) — and then I can base64 it and run the full local smoke test.

One note: **only the Account Holder** (or an Admin) of the Apple Developer team can create Developer ID certs. If the "Developer ID Application" option is greyed out or missing, that's a permissions issue on your Apple Developer membership, not a mistake on your end — tell me and we'll sort it.

Swift Package Certificate
Sign Swift packages and package collections for distribution. For use with Swift Package Manager v5.9 or later.

Establish connectivity between your notification server, the Apple Push Notification service sandbox, and production environment to update ClockKit complication data. # Release Setup

deadreckon releases are built by GitHub Actions through `cargo-dist`.
Pushing a version tag starts the release workflow; ordinary pushes and pull
requests run the `dist plan` check without publishing anything.

macOS artifacts are signed with a Developer ID Application certificate and
notarized through Apple's `notarytool` service. The one-time setup to obtain
that certificate and wire the secrets is at the bottom of this document
([Apple Developer ID setup](#apple-developer-id-setup-one-time)).

## Required Apple Secrets

macOS artifacts are signed and notarized when the repository has these GitHub
Actions secrets configured:

| Secret | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `APPLE_CERT_P12` | Base64-encoded Developer ID Application `.p12` certificate export (certificate **and** private key). |
| `APPLE_CERT_PWD` | Password used when exporting the `.p12` certificate. |
| `APPLE_ID` | Apple Developer account email used by `notarytool`. See the note below — this is the Apple ID that **owns the Developer membership**, which may differ from your git/commit email. |
| `APPLE_TEAM_ID` | Apple Developer Team ID (the 10-character code, e.g. shown in parentheses in the certificate name). |
| `APPLE_APP_PWD` | App-specific password (not the account password) for the Apple ID used by `notarytool`. |

> **Apple ID gotcha.** `APPLE_ID` must be the Apple ID under which the Developer
> Program membership lives *and* under which the app-specific password was
> generated. If these do not match the team, `notarytool` fails with
> `HTTP status code: 401. Invalid credentials`. This is frequently a different
> address than the work/commit email.

If `APPLE_CERT_P12` is not present, the workflow currently skips macOS signing
and notarization with a warning. That keeps forks and dry-runs usable, but
release notes for any unsigned macOS artifact must call out that it is unsigned.
(Per the Release Trust rider, official RC/stable tags on the canonical repo are
intended to fail closed when signing material is missing rather than publish
unsigned — track that in the rider, not here.)

## Package Manager Secrets

The package-manager publishing jobs expect these additional repository secrets:

| Secret | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `NPM_TOKEN` | npm automation token with publish rights for `deadreckon` and the five `deadreckon-*` platform packages. |
| `HOMEBREW_TAP_TOKEN` | GitHub token with push rights to `gdc/homebrew-tap`. |

## Current Secret Status

The five Apple secrets and the package-manager secrets are configured as
repository secrets in GitHub Actions. Secret **values** are never stored in this
repository — list names only with `gh secret list`. Do not commit certificates,
passwords, Team IDs, or Apple IDs to git.

Local signing material (`*.p12`, `*.cer`, `*.certSigningRequest`, `developer-id*`)
is covered by `.gitignore` and must stay out of version control.

## Release Flow

1. Confirm `cargo build --release`, `cargo test --workspace`, `cargo clippy
   --workspace -- -D warnings`, and `cargo fmt --check` are green.
2. Confirm the Apple, npm, and Homebrew secrets above are configured before
   creating a public release (`gh secret list`).
3. Optionally run the [local notarization smoke test](#local-notarization-smoke-test)
   to prove the signing chain end to end before pushing a tag.
4. Create the release tag locally.
5. Push the tag to GitHub. The release workflow builds five target artifacts,
   signs and notarizes the two macOS binaries when secrets are present, builds
   shell and PowerShell installers, publishes the GitHub release, updates the
   Homebrew tap, and publishes the npm wrapper/platform packages.

The agent should not push tags. The first real release remains an operator
action.

# Apple Developer ID setup (one time)

This section records how to obtain the Developer ID Application certificate and
wire the GitHub secrets. It only needs to be done once per signing certificate
(certificates are valid ~5 years). All concrete identifiers (Team ID, Apple ID,
passwords) are intentionally omitted — they live only in GitHub secrets.

## Prerequisites

- Membership in the Apple Developer Program, with **Account Holder or Admin**
  role (only these roles can create Developer ID certificates).
- macOS with Keychain Access and Xcode command-line tools (`codesign`,
  `xcrun notarytool`).

## 1. Create the certificate signing request (CSR)

In **Keychain Access** → menu bar **Certificate Assistant → Request a
Certificate From a Certificate Authority**:

- User Email Address: the Apple ID email.
- Common Name: any label (e.g. "DeadReckon Developer ID").
- CA Email Address: leave blank.
- Select **Saved to disk**.

This generates a private key in the login keychain and a
`.certSigningRequest` file. The CSR is not secret; the private key stays in the
keychain.

## 2. Create the certificate at Apple

At <https://developer.apple.com/account/resources/certificates/list>:

1. **+** → **Developer ID Application** (not "Apple Development", not "Developer
   ID Installer", not any "Mac App" / "Distribution" variant — only this one
   signs binaries for distribution outside the App Store).
2. Intermediary: choose **G2 Sub-CA (Xcode 11.4.1 or later)**.
3. Upload the `.certSigningRequest` from step 1.
4. Download the resulting `.cer` and double-click it to install into the login
   keychain.

## 3. Install the Developer ID G2 intermediate (avoids "0 valid identities")

A freshly installed Developer ID cert often shows as **"not trusted"** in
Keychain Access, and `security find-identity -v -p codesigning` reports
`0 valid identities found`. This is because the **Developer ID G2 intermediate
CA** is missing, so the trust chain cannot be built. Install it:

\```bash
curl -fsSL -o /tmp/DeveloperIDG2CA.cer \
  https://www.apple.com/certificateauthority/DeveloperIDG2CA.cer
security import /tmp/DeveloperIDG2CA.cer -k "$HOME/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db"
security find-identity -v -p codesigning   # should now list 1 valid identity
\```

(Apple's full set of intermediates is at
<https://www.apple.com/certificateauthority/>.)

## 4. Export the `.p12`

In **Keychain Access → My Certificates**, expand the "Developer ID Application:
…" entry so the nested **private key** is visible. Select **both** the
certificate and the key, right-click → **Export 2 items… → Personal Information
Exchange (.p12)**. Choose an export password — this becomes `APPLE_CERT_PWD`.

Validate the export contains the private key (run in a real terminal; the prompt
is hidden):

\```bash
read -rs P && echo && \
  openssl pkcs12 -in Certificates.p12 -nocerts -noout -passin pass:"$P" \
  && echo "ok: key loads" || echo "wrong password or no key"; unset P
\```

## 5. Create the app-specific password

At <https://appleid.apple.com> → **Sign-In and Security → App-Specific
Passwords → +**. Label it (e.g. "deadreckon notarytool") and save the generated
`xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx` value — this becomes `APPLE_APP_PWD`. Generate it while
signed in as the Apple ID that owns the Developer membership (see the Apple ID
gotcha above).

## 6. Set the GitHub secrets

Base64-encode the `.p12` and pipe it straight into the secret so the value never
echoes:

\```bash
base64 -i Certificates.p12 | tr -d '\n' | gh secret set APPLE_CERT_P12
gh secret set APPLE_ID         # the membership-owning Apple ID email
gh secret set APPLE_TEAM_ID    # the 10-character Team ID
gh secret set APPLE_APP_PWD    # the app-specific password
gh secret set APPLE_CERT_PWD   # the .p12 export password (prompts hidden)
gh secret list                 # confirm all five are present
\```

Prefer the hidden prompt (`gh secret set NAME` then paste) for any value you do
not want in shell history.

## Local notarization smoke test

Prove the full chain (sign → notarize) locally before trusting CI. Signing uses
the keychain identity directly and needs no password; notarization needs the
Apple ID, Team ID, and app-specific password.

\```bash
work=$(mktemp -d)
cp target/release/deadreckon "$work/deadreckon"

# sign with hardened runtime + secure timestamp
codesign --force --sign "Developer ID Application" \
  --options runtime --timestamp "$work/deadreckon"
codesign --verify --verbose "$work/deadreckon"
codesign --display --verbose=2 "$work/deadreckon"   # expect Developer ID + Apple Root chain

# before notarization, Gatekeeper rejects with "Unnotarized Developer ID" — expected
spctl --assess --type execute --verbose "$work/deadreckon" || true

# notarize (fill in the three values; do not commit them)
ditto -c -k --keepParent "$work/deadreckon" "$work/deadreckon.zip"
xcrun notarytool submit "$work/deadreckon.zip" \
  --apple-id   "<membership Apple ID>" \
  --team-id    "<team id>" \
  --password   "<app-specific password>" \
  --wait
\```

A successful run prints `status: Accepted`. Note: a standalone binary cannot be
`stapler staple`d (stapling applies to `.app`/`.dmg`/`.pkg`); the notarization
ticket is served online, which is sufficient for the distributed binary.

## Rotation and cleanup

- App-specific passwords and `.p12` exports are revocable. If a secret value is
  ever exposed (pasted into a chat, a log, etc.), revoke it at the source
  (appleid.apple.com for app passwords, the certificate list for certs) and
  re-run the relevant `gh secret set`.
- Delete local signing material when finished: `rm Certificates.p12
  developerID_application.cer CertificateSigningRequest.certSigningRequest`.

# One-time setup steps (procedure)

### 1. Apple Developer Program ($99/yr)

- Enroll: https://developer.apple.com/programs/enroll/
- Use a long-lived Apple ID — this becomes `APPLE_ID`. **It must be the Apple ID
  that owns the membership** (here: `gregce@gmail.com`).
- **Individual** enrollment is instant-ish after payment; **Organization** needs
  a D-U-N-S number and takes 1–14 days. Individual is fine for a personal CLI;
  the cert shows your name in Gatekeeper output.

### 2. Create the CSR (Keychain Access)

- Keychain Access → menu bar **Certificate Assistant → Request a Certificate
  From a Certificate Authority**.
- User Email Address: the Apple ID email. Common Name: any label.
- CA Email Address: blank. Select **Saved to disk**.
- Produces a `.certSigningRequest`; the private key is created in the login
  keychain.

### 3. Create the Developer ID Application certificate

- https://developer.apple.com/account/resources/certificates → `+` →
  **Developer ID Application** (not "Apple Development", not "Developer ID
  Installer", not any "Mac App"/"Distribution" variant).
- Intermediary: **G2 Sub-CA (Xcode 11.4.1 or later)**.
- Upload the CSR, download the `.cer`, double-click to install into the login
  keychain.

### 4. Install the Developer ID G2 intermediate

Avoids the "0 valid identities" / "not trusted" trap (see gotcha above):

\```bash
curl -fsSL -o /tmp/DeveloperIDG2CA.cer \
  https://www.apple.com/certificateauthority/DeveloperIDG2CA.cer
security import /tmp/DeveloperIDG2CA.cer -k "$HOME/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db"
security find-identity -v -p codesigning
\```

### 5. Export the `.p12` for CI

- Keychain Access → My Certificates → expand "Developer ID Application: …" so the
  nested private key shows → select **both** rows → right-click → **Export 2
  items… → Personal Information Exchange (.p12)**.
- Set an export password → this is `APPLE_CERT_PWD`.

\```bash
base64 -i Certificates.p12 | tr -d '\n' | gh secret set APPLE_CERT_P12
# or: ... | pbcopy  and paste into the GitHub secret
\```

### 6. App-specific password for `notarytool`

## Local verification before trusting CI

Sign with the keychain identity (no password needed), then notarize:

\```bash

cp target/release/deadreckon "$work/deadreckon"

codesign --force --sign "Developer ID Application" \
  --options runtime --timestamp "$work/deadreckon"
codesign --verify --verbose "$work/deadreckon"
# expect: "satisfies its Designated Requirement"
codesign --display --verbose=2 "$work/deadreckon"
# expect Authority chain: Developer ID Application → Developer ID CA → Apple Root CA

spctl --assess --type execute --verbose "$work/deadreckon" || true
# before notarization: "rejected — Unnotarized Developer ID" is EXPECTED

ditto -c -k --keepParent "$work/deadreckon" "$work/deadreckon.zip"
xcrun notarytool submit "$work/deadreckon.zip" \
  --apple-id "gregce@gmail.com" \
  --team-id  "4GRQMF5T5U" \
  --password "lbyn-dvnh-xnif-pyjh" \
  --wait
# expect: status: Accepted
\```

- **No stapling for raw binaries.** A CLI (not an `.app`/`.dmg`/`.pkg`) can only
  be notarized, not stapled. Gatekeeper does an online ticket check on first run;
  that's the expected flow.
- **`--options runtime` is required.** Notarization rejects submissions without
  the hardened runtime flag.

- **Keychain on CI runners.** The workflow creates a temporary keychain, imports

Still pending on Apple. Now to your real question — and it's the right one to ask, because **signing and the `curl | bash` installer are two different things that people constantly conflate.**

## Short answer

**No, signing/notarization does not *create* that install line — but it's the thing that makes the installed binary actually run cleanly.** They're complementary layers:

- **The `curl … | bash` install script** = the *distribution mechanism* (how the bits get onto the machine and onto `PATH`).
- **Code signing + notarization** = the *trust mechanism* (whether macOS lets the bits execute without a scary "Apple cannot verify this / unidentified developer" wall).

You need both for a polished product, but they solve different problems.

## What the install script actually is

That `entire.io/install.sh` is just a hosted shell script that, when piped to `bash`:
1. Detects the user's OS + CPU arch (`uname`).
2. Downloads the matching prebuilt archive from your **GitHub Releases**.
3. Verifies a checksum.
4. Extracts the binary and drops it in `~/.local/bin` (or similar) and nudges `PATH`.

**You already generate this.** Your `release.yml` builds "shell and PowerShell installers" — that's cargo-dist producing exactly this `install.sh`. cargo-dist hosts it at a GitHub URL like:

```
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://github.com/gregce/deadreckon/releases/latest/download/deadreckon-installer.sh | sh
```

To get the *pretty* `curl https://yourdomain/install.sh | bash`, you just point a domain/redirect (e.g. a Vercel/Cloudflare rewrite at `entire.io/install.sh`) at that cargo-dist installer URL. That's a DNS/hosting task, **not** a signing task.

## So where does signing come in? The crucial subtlety

Here's the part most people get wrong, and it's genuinely good news for you:

**`curl`/`wget` do NOT set the macOS quarantine flag.** The `com.apple.quarantine` attribute — the thing that triggers Gatekeeper's "unidentified developer, cannot be opened" wall — is applied by **browsers, Mail, AirDrop, and archive utilities**, not by command-line downloads. So a binary that arrives via `curl | bash` typically runs **even if it's unsigned**, because Gatekeeper never gets invoked on it.

That means: *for the curl-pipe-bash path specifically, signing is not strictly required to make it work today.*

## Then why did we just do all this signing work? Because the curl path isn't your only path:

| Install path | Quarantined? | Needs signing/notarization? |
|---|---|---|
| `curl … \| bash` | No | Not strictly — runs unsigned |
| **Browser download** from your GitHub Releases page | **Yes** | **Yes** — blocked without it |
| **`.dmg` / `.pkg`** | Yes | Yes |
| **Homebrew** (`brew install`) | Varies; casks check | Yes for casks/notarization-aware flows |
| **npm wrapper** postinstall | No (curl-like) | Not strictly |

And beyond the table, signing/notarization buys you:

1. **Browser & Homebrew users** — a huge fraction of people *will* land on your GitHub Releases page and click the binary, or `brew install`. Those break hard without notarization.
2. **Professional trust** — `codesign --verify` passes, the binary shows *your verified identity* ("Gregory Ceccarelli"), and there's no "this app is from an unidentified developer" dialog ever.
3. **Future-proofing** — Apple keeps tightening Gatekeeper. The curl-bypass-quarantine loophole is a behavior, not a guarantee; signing is the durable answer.
4. **Tamper-evidence** — the signature + notarization ticket prove the binary is the one you built and Apple scanned, unmodified.

## Bottom line for what you're building

To ship the `curl … | bash` experience like Entire/Bun/Rust do, you need, in order:

1. **The installer script** — ✅ cargo-dist already generates it; you mainly need to host it at a clean URL (DNS/redirect work).
2. **Prebuilt binaries on GitHub Releases** — ✅ your `release.yml` builds 5 targets.
3. **Signed + notarized macOS binaries** — ✅ what we just set up; *not* needed for the curl path itself, but essential the moment anyone downloads via browser, `.dmg`, or Homebrew, and it makes the whole thing trustworthy.
4. **Checksums** so `install.sh` can verify integrity — your rider already mandates `SHA256SUMS`.

So: **signing doesn't enable the install line — your installer script does that — but signing is what makes "downloaded it, it just ran, no warnings" true across *every* channel, not just the curl one.** They're partners, and you want both.

- **This is the modern path.** `notarytool` replaced the old `altool --notarize-app`, which is deprecated. Your `release.yml` uses `notarytool` too, so the CI does exactly what we just rehearsed locally.
- **One thing CI does that our local test skips:** after a successful notarization, the real release path can `xcrun stapler staple` the ticket onto the artifact — **but** that only works on `.app`/`.dmg`/`.pkg` bundles, *not* a bare CLI binary like `deadreckon`. For a raw binary the ticket lives on Apple's servers and Gatekeeper checks it online on first run. So "no stapling" is expected and fine here.

Still pending — genuinely an unusually slow run from Apple today (more on that below). Here's the honest timing picture:

## No — this run is an outlier, not the norm

**Typical notarization is 1–5 minutes**, often under 2. Apple's own guidance says ~90% complete within ~5 min. What we're seeing right now (15+ min) is Apple's notary service having a slow day — it happens periodically and is on *their* side, nothing about your setup. You can even check their status at [Apple System Status](https://developer.apple.com/system-status/) ("Developer ID Notary Service"). First-ever submissions for a new account also sometimes run slower.

## More importantly: CI does NOT run this on "every build"

This is the key thing to internalize — notarization only happens on **release tags**, not on every commit or PR:

| Trigger | What runs | Notarization? |
|---|---|---|
| Push to branch / open PR | `dist plan` check only | ❌ none |
| Every commit | nothing release-y | ❌ none |
| **RC tag** `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` | full build + sign + notarize | ✅ once |
| **Stable tag** `vX.Y.Z` | full build + sign + notarize + publish | ✅ once |

So your day-to-day `cargo build`, your pushes, your PRs — **zero notarization, zero added latency.** You only pay this cost when you cut an actual release, which is occasional.

## And even on a release, it's not serial

When it does run in CI:
- The two macOS targets (`aarch64` + `x86_64`) notarize **in parallel** as separate matrix jobs, so it's *one* notarization wait, not two stacked.
- It overlaps with the rest of the release pipeline (Linux/Windows builds, installer generation, etc.).
- A normal release's notarization adds maybe **2–5 min** to a release that already takes ~10–20 min to build all 5 targets. It's a small slice of total release time, not a per-build tax.

## So in practice

- **Developing:** no notarization, ever. Fast.
- **Cutting a release:** notarization adds a few minutes, runs in parallel, happens maybe weekly/monthly. Today's 15-min crawl is a bad-Apple-day outlier you'll rarely see.

One safety note for CI: it's worth setting a generous **timeout** on the notarize step (e.g. 30 min) so a slow-Apple day like today fails loudly rather than hanging a runner indefinitely — your `release.yml` uses `--wait`, which will block exactly like we're seeing. Want me to check whether that step has a timeout once the verdict's in?

_**Agent (claude-opus-4-8 2026-06-01 23:53:22Z)**_

Honest answer: **there's no real web dashboard for notarization.** Unlike App Store submissions, the Developer ID notary service is **API/CLI-only** — Apple never built a browser UI for it. `developer.apple.com` and App Store Connect won't show this submission. So the CLI is the canonical view.

But there are two ways for *you* to see the same thing I see:

## 1. Email (the closest thing to a "web" view) 📧
Apple **emails the result** to the Apple ID when notarization completes — so **`gregce@gmail.com` will get a "Your Mac software was successfully notarized" (or rejected) email** with the submission ID. Check that inbox; it lands the moment the verdict resolves. That's effectively your at-a-glance status without a terminal.

## 2. Run the same CLI commands yourself
You can run these in your own terminal — or type them here with the `!` prefix to run them in this session:

```bash
# the same authoritative history I keep checking:
xcrun notarytool history \
  --apple-id "gregce@gmail.com" --team-id "4GRQMF5T5U" --password "lbyn-dvnh-xnif-pyjh"

# status of just this submission:
xcrun notarytool info 45990da3-52a2-4274-b47f-ec3ad88701f5 \
  --apple-id "gregce@gmail.com" --team-id "4GRQMF5T5U" --password "lbyn-dvnh-xnif-pyjh"

# once it finishes — the detailed JSON log (issues, hashes, etc.):
xcrun notarytool log 45990da3-52a2-4274-b47f-ec3ad88701f5 \
  --apple-id "gregce@gmail.com" --team-id "4GRQMF5T5U" --password "lbyn-dvnh-xnif-pyjh"
```

`history`/`info` return the same `status: In Progress / Accepted / Invalid` I've been relaying. `log` only works after a terminal verdict and gives the full breakdown (useful if it ever comes back `Invalid`).

> Tip: to avoid putting the password on the command line each time, you can store it once with `xcrun notarytool store-credentials` (it saves a named keychain profile), then use `--keychain-profile <name>` instead of the three `--apple-id/--team-id/--password` flags. Handy for repeated local checks.

So: **watch `gregce@gmail.com`'s inbox** for the push-style notification, or run `notarytool info <id>` anytime for the live status. I'm still holding on the `--wait` process and will report the instant it flips.

Here's exactly what got submitted:

## Contents of `deadreckon.zip`

```
dr-notary.eMmM/deadreckon       15,402,128 bytes   ← the signed binary
dr-notary.eMmM/._deadreckon            163 bytes   ← macOS metadata sidecar
```

**1. `deadreckon`** — the real payload: a **15.4 MB arm64 Mach-O executable** (your native Apple Silicon release build, `target/release/deadreckon`), carrying the signature Apple is scanning:
```
Authority=Developer ID Application: Gregory Ceccarelli (4GRQMF5T5U)
Authority=Developer ID Certification Authority
Authority=Apple Root CA          ← full trust chain
flags=0x10000(runtime)           ← hardened runtime
Timestamp=Jun 1, 2026 7:15:25 PM ← Apple secure timestamp
```

**2. `._deadreckon`** — a 163-byte **AppleDouble sidecar**. `ditto` auto-creates these `._`-prefixed files to preserve extended attributes/metadata when zipping. It's harmless macOS cruft; Apple's notary service ignores `._` files. (You'll see these whenever you `ditto`/zip on a Mac.)

Two things worth noting for when this is the *real* CI flow:

- **The nested `dr-notary.eMmM/` folder** is there because `ditto --keepParent` preserved the parent directory name — and here the parent was our random tempdir. In a proper release, cargo-dist names that parent sensibly (e.g. the archive root). For *notarization* it doesn't matter — the notary service just walks the zip, finds the Mach-O, and scans it regardless of folder name.
- **This was arm64 only.** We signed/submitted just the native Apple Silicon binary. CI does the **x86_64** target as a *separate* build → sign → notarize in its own matrix job. So a full release notarizes two binaries (in parallel), not one.
